A1.justification: Both PDFs describe CLASH with the same title, authors, and benchmark. Their complete main texts, appendices A–F, tables, figures, and equations support reliable comparison despite additions and layout changes.

before.justification: v3 reports original evaluations of 14 models, human annotation results, reasoning-chain analyses, and steerability experiments in the main text and appendices.

after.justification: v4 retains these original empirical results and adds dynamic-overcommitment analysis and an all-pairs steerability experiment.

M1.justification: The CLASH construction pipeline, character categories, evaluation questions, value-mapping procedure, and conditional-steerability calculation remain unchanged. Algorithm 1 is retained; the added diagnostic and newly disclosed prompt do not establish a change to the proposed method.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same 345 dilemmas, 3,795 perspectives, four domains, and static/dynamic tasks. The all-pairs analysis changes aggregation and selection within existing coverage; dynamic scenarios were already evaluated in v3.

E2.justification: The 14 evaluated models, human comparison, and random reference remain unchanged. Figure 4 retains the Claude, Deepseek, and Qwen families. Newly cited methods in Section 5 are not added as evaluated comparators.

E3.justification: Appendix D.4 adds a steerability rerun using all value pairs except those with base preference 0 or 1, alongside the retained greater-than-16-occurrence selection. A new prompt judges overcommitment in current-perspective reasoning. Main benchmark settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: The new all-pairs robustness check directly tests dependence on the frequency cutoff and finds that the reported preference–steerability correlation loses significance. Section 4.2 and Figure 4 also extend failure analysis to overcommitment in dynamic perspectives, substantially strengthening the supplementary investigation.

E5.justification: The three repetitions in Appendix A.2 and existing correlation and Wilcoxon testing practices remain. Appendix D.4 adds significance outcomes for another analysis, without introducing new statistical procedures, seed information, run-count reporting, or uncertainty intervals.

E6.justification: Both versions retain the filtered correlation r = -0.243, p < 0.005. v4 additionally reports r = 0.046, p = 0.364 under all-pairs selection, materially qualifying that finding; Qwen and Llama correlations also become nonsignificant. Figure 4 revises existing cognitive and ethical-theory percentages and adds dynamic-overcommitment results. Benchmark accuracy tables remain unchanged.

T1.justification: The preference definitions, steerability ratios, and Algorithm 1 are unchanged. Neither version contains mathematical theorems or proofs. The added dynamic-overcommitment description is an operational diagnostic, not a new formal mathematical result.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same benchmark contributions and principal findings. In particular, the broad preference–steerability correlation claim remains despite the new nonsignificant all-pairs result.

C2.justification: v4 interprets dynamic overcommitment as excessive adherence to a character’s previous perspective. Its expanded Ethics Statement replaces the brief sensitive-content warning with explicit applicability limits: CLASH is diagnostic, and high scores alone do not establish suitability for deployment in high-stakes environments.

D1.justification: New Figure 34 supplies the exact base-preference prompt, previously described only generally. Figure 30 supplies the dynamic-overcommitment judging prompt, and Figure 4’s caption newly specifies averaging within model families. These improve documentation without establishing changes to retained experimental settings.

R1.justification: Section 5 substantially expands research positioning. It introduces a ground-truth-versus-preference taxonomy and positions CLASH as bridging those approaches, then rewrites the steering comparison around multi-objective alignment and conflicting-value prioritization. Added works include Backmann, Cheung, Kumar and Jurgens, Wu, Zhou, Vamplew, Gupta, and Ryan.

P1.justification: Rewriting is concentrated in Related Work and the Ethics Statement, with limited edits elsewhere. RQ2 now clearly asks about detecting human discomfort, and appendix subsections are inserted or regrouped. The overall narrative and most existing text remain intact.

P2.justification: Figure 4a gains a dynamic-overcommitment panel and revised labels and caption; Figure 4b changes its legend placement and proportions. Two prompt figures are added. Existing appendix figures and Algorithm 1 are redistributed and renumbered, while table structures remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: v4 improves transparency and reproducibility through the all-pairs robustness check, additional diagnostic evidence, exact base-preference prompt, and clearer deployment limitations. However, the new check finds no significant overall correlation while the abstract and conclusion retain the broad correlation claim. The additions make the evidence more assessable, but this unresolved qualification limits the overall gain.
